passage:
At sixteen, Omkar had a geography project and a whole month to finish it. He kept saying, "I'll begin on Saturday." If he tried and the map came out crooked, his teacher would see that he was not good at this. Doing nothing kept the picture of himself intact. The night before, he pasted a rushed collage and got a weak mark.

At twenty-five, at his first office job, Omkar noticed the same heavy feeling as a report deadline crept closer. This time he closed the game he had opened and asked himself, "What exactly is uncomfortable? Is it that I'm scared it won't be good? Is it that I don't know the first step? Or is it just dull?" He wrote the answer on a sticky note: "I don't know what the client wants."

He turned to his colleague Varun. "Can I ask you two questions about the brief?" Varun nodded, and the fog began to lift.

qa.q: What did Omkar write on his sticky note?
qa.a: He wrote, "I don't know what the client wants."

qa.q: What has changed in how Omkar handles delay between sixteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At sixteen he avoids starting to protect his image, and the work suffers; at twenty-five he asks what exactly is uncomfortable, names the real feeling as unclear steps, and asks Varun for help.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he put off the geography map at sixteen?
qa.a: Omkar was afraid of looking bad, since a crooked map might show his teacher he was not good at it.

qa.q: Why did naming the feeling help Omkar at twenty-five?
qa.a: Naming it as not knowing what the client wanted separated the feeling from the whole task and pointed to a fix, asking Varun about the brief.

grounding: Procrastination linked across ages: a teenager avoiding a project for fear of judgement, and a young professional naming the real feeling behind delay and asking for help.
